extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and practitioners in patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when a 'principle' (truth of science, law of nature, or rule of practice) is or is not the subject-matter of a patent, how it must be embodied, how claims must be framed, and how infringement/substantial similarity is assessed. Focuses on specification, claim breadth, and jury considerations in infringement disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: You cannot patent a principle alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The law says you cannot take out a patent for a principle, that is, for a barren principle; a mere idea or principle alone cannot support a patent and, if the principle alone be the foundation of the patent, the patent must be void ab initio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the general principle or effect of steam was known before Watt; if only the principle is claimed, the patent is invalid. A principle must be clothed with form (an embodiment) to be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle reduced into practice = practice/manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'principle reduced into practice' means a practice founded on principle — the thing done or made (the manufacture) which is invented. The patent is for the mode of carrying the principle into actual effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Buller's formulation: you can patent the principle only when it has been embodied in some practical mode described in the specification; the invention for which letters-patent can issue is the working or making of some manner of new manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must embody principle in a mode/machine to claim it
rubrics_metrics.description: You may take out a patent for the spirit of your invention if you have clothed it with a form, given it body and substance (i.e., embodied the principle in a machine, method, or manufacture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor has described a practical mode of carrying the principle into effect, the patent is for that mode or machine; others who devise different machines do not infringe unless their machine is a colorable imitation. Example: Watt's patent — protection was for his mode embodied in a machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of 'principles' (truths, laws, rules of practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles fall into varieties: truths of exact (mathematical) science, laws of natural science (derived from observation/experiment), and rules of practice (derived from human arrangement). These classes are essentially distinct for patent purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Hadley's quadrant (geometry + optics) and Dollond's achromatic lens (optical laws) are applications of scientific truths; Arkwright, Jupe, Galloway examples illustrate rules of practice. The class affects how the principle is regarded and appropriated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of appropriation of laws or truths determined case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: While truths of exact science or laws of natural science cannot themselves be owned, the extent to which an inventor may appropriate the application of such a truth or law is determined by a jury on the particular circumstances; general rules cannot be laid down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No universal rule — courts and juries assess whether subsequent applications constitute piracy of the original application. The answer depends on the nature of the embodiment and the degree of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must particularly describe nature and means
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the principle be given to the world and that the means should be fully described, and that the means, as described, be sufficient for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with the proviso requires that the inventor particularly describe and ascertain the nature of his invention and how it is to be performed; mere announcement of the idea is insufficient. Failure to disclose general rule/principle (or to give sufficient means) reduces the legal protection and the public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad claims ('every shape' or 'from whatever source') risk claiming a principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is so framed as to claim every shape or every source of a property (e.g., 'elasticity to backs of cards from whatever source derived'), it amounts to a claim for a principle and is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson & Walton examples: claiming 'every shape' equates to claiming the principle itself. The inventor must claim some specific mode of doing it; otherwise the claim may be treated as claiming the principle and be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent may cover principle coupled with a novel mode of carrying it into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: You may take out a patent for a principle coupled with the mode of carrying the principle into effect, provided you have not only discovered the principle but also invented some mode of carrying it into effect and described it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practical mode has been invented and disclosed, the inventor can seek protection against other modes that a jury would deem a piracy or colorable imitation of the original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method- or mode-only claims insufficient without practical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to support a patent for a method only without having carried it into effect and produced some new substance; the mere application or mode of using a thing is not sufficient ground unless realized in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court commentary: claiming a method without showing carrying into effect (and producing something concrete) will not support patentability. The 'method' must result in or be embodied in a manufacture or operative apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement assessment: colorable variation vs substantial independent invention
rubrics_metrics.description: In infringement contests the question is whether a subsequently invented and adopted mode is a substantial and independent invention or only a colorable variation borrowed from the previous invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements for jury consideration include: character of original invention, merit to be attributed to its author, the means by which the principle is carried out, the object of its application and the end attained, the success and utility of the prior invention, and the comparative merits of the two inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverer of a principle has higher merit though legal extent of property is same
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who discovers a new truth or law and applies it is of higher merit than one who merely applies prior-known knowledge; however, the legal property acquired does not differ in extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, juries may favor the discoverer when assessing infringement and equitable considerations, but statutory rights are of the same theoretical extent as other inventors who apply known principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of principle in specification undermines protection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the principle is kept back and only certain arrangements without any general rule are given to the world, then either the invention is a mere accident of small merit or, if by design, the inventor fails to comply with the law and loses potential protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design to conceal reduces public benefit and may result in failing to secure the full extent of protection which could have been obtained had the principle and sufficient means been disclosed.
